h3.h3: How is cost per hire formally defined?

evidence.gloss: Basic definition of cost per hire
evidence.verbatim: Cost per hire (CPH) is a standardized recruiting metric that captures the average amount an organization spends to fill one open position, combining both the money paid to outside vendors and the internal labor and overhead consumed by the hiring process[1].

evidence.gloss: SHRM/ANSI formal definition of CPH
evidence.verbatim: The formal definition, set by the SHRM/ANSI 06001.2012 standard, states CPH as "the mean average of total costs divided by the number of hires"[1].

evidence.gloss: LinkedIn's definition of CPH
evidence.verbatim: LinkedIn's recruiting metrics guide describes it in similar terms: total spend associated with filling an open position (recruiter fees, advertisements, etc.) divided by the number of hires[1].

evidence.gloss: CPH as a simple average framing
evidence.verbatim: In practice, this is a straightforward average — how much money it takes, on average, to hire one person[1].

evidence.gloss: Direct-cost/indirect-cost split with examples, tied to a business case (up to 30% cost cut)
evidence.verbatim: One source lays out a direct-cost/indirect-cost split — direct costs being visible and measurable (job advertising, background checks, recruiter fees, onboarding expenses) and indirect costs being harder to quantify but equally impactful (lost productivity, knowledge gaps from departing employees, time spent re-engaging candidates, team disruption from unfilled positions) — and ties this framework to a business case, noting that streamlining hiring can cut costs by up to 30%[29].

evidence.gloss: Another source explicitly scopes CPH to include specific internal and external costs, excluding post-hire training/ramp time
evidence.verbatim: Another source is explicit about scope: cost per hire "includes all internal costs such as recruiter time, hiring manager interview time, HR coordination, and prorated ATS or recruiting software subscriptions" plus "all external costs: job board fees, agency and staffing fees, background checks, assessments, and referral bonuses," while explicitly excluding post-hire training costs and productivity ramp time, which "belong" to a separate calculation[16].

evidence.verbatim: This same source goes further than most by distinguishing allocatable internal time from invoiceable external spend for Finance-auditability purposes

evidence.gloss: One definition explicitly excludes post-hire training costs and productivity ramp time from CPH
evidence.verbatim: One definition specifies that CPH "includes all internal costs such as recruiter time, hiring manager interview time, HR coordination, and prorated ATS or recruiting software subscriptions" plus external costs like "job board fees, agency and staffing fees, background checks, assessments, and referral bonuses" — but states plainly "it does not include post-hire training costs or productivity ramp time"[16].

evidence.verbatim: Ramp-up time is described elsewhere as "not just a talent challenge, it is a critical variable in workforce planning and ROI," yet it sits outside the standard calculation[13].

sections.h2: What does the ANSI/SHRM Cost-Per-Hire standard actually require?

h3.h3: What is the standard formula for cost per hire?

evidence.gloss: The accepted CPH formula
evidence.verbatim: Cost per Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) / Total Number of Hires in a given time period[3][19][1]

evidence.gloss: Formula standardized in 2012 by SHRM/ANSI
evidence.verbatim: This formula was formally standardized in 2012 through a collaboration between the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), producing the ANSI/SHRM 06001.2012 standard[9][3][1].

evidence.gloss: Scope boundary of the standard
evidence.verbatim: The standard is bounded specifically to activities relating to sourcing, recruiting, and staffing costs, whether external or internal, out of pocket or otherwise[9].

evidence.gloss: Cost per hire is codified by a national standard, not informal
evidence.verbatim: Cost per hire is not an informal metric — it is codified by a national standard.

evidence.gloss: SHRM/ANSI Cost-Per-Hire standard formula definition
evidence.verbatim: The SHRM/ANSI Cost-Per-Hire standard, developed with the American National Standards Institute, defines the formula as (Total Internal Costs + Total External Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires[23][10][11].

evidence.gloss: The industry-standard CPH formula
evidence.verbatim: The baseline, widely cited formula for cost per hire (CPH) is straightforward: CPH = (External Costs + Internal Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires in a Time Period[19].

evidence.gloss: CPH is codified in the ANSI/SHRM standard
evidence.verbatim: This is codified in the American National Standard ANSI/SHRM 06001:2012, a 50-page document whose purpose is to get HR and Finance departments to agree on how this single quotient should be assembled[9][19].

evidence.gloss: CPH is bounded to sourcing/recruiting/staffing costs regardless of type
evidence.verbatim: According to this standard, the CPH metric is bounded specifically by activities relating to sourcing, recruiting, and staffing costs — whether those costs are external or internal, and whether they are out-of-pocket or otherwise[9].

evidence.gloss: Standard defines the CPHI formula
evidence.verbatim: That standard defines the Cost-per-Hire Index (CPHI) formula as measuring "the costs associated with the sourcing, recruiting, and staffing" function[4]

evidence.gloss: The core CPH equation
evidence.verbatim: Nearly every source that defines CPH converges on the same core equation: **Cost-Per-Hire = (Total Internal Recruiting Costs + Total External Recruiting Costs) ÷ Total Number of Hires** in a given time period[3][17].

evidence.gloss: Formula inputs and time-window requirement
evidence.verbatim: The formula has two inputs feeding the numerator (internal and external costs) and one feeding the denominator (the count of hires), and all three must be tied to the same time window for the number to be meaningful[3].

evidence.gloss: SHRM/ANSI treated as industry-standard baseline, has harmonized the metric
evidence.verbatim: This SHRM/ANSI definition is treated as the industry-standard baseline, and while the scope of included costs can vary slightly by organization, "the SHRM standard has largely harmonized the metric's calculation across the HR field"[17].

evidence.gloss: CPH base formula (ANSI/SHRM model)
evidence.verbatim: Cost-Per-Hire = (Total Internal Costs + Total External Costs) / Total Hires × 100 (implied CPH base formula)

evidence.gloss: SHRM/ANSI standard established common approach, adopted by most large orgs
evidence.verbatim: "The SHRM/ANSI standard has gone a long way toward establishing a common approach, and most large organizations adhere to it or a very similar methodology,"

evidence.gloss: Widely agreed-upon definition in principle: CPH = total recruiting costs per hire
evidence.verbatim: "we can say there is a widely agreed-upon definition in principle (CPH = total recruiting costs per hire)"[17]

evidence.gloss: The standard's formula definition and required practices (representative sample, consistent time period)
evidence.verbatim: The standard itself contains a formal formula definition (Section 7.1 FORMULA DEFINITION) and prescribes actions that must be taken to maintain quality and transparency when calculating cost-per-hire, including creating a representative sample and constraining the metric within a consistent time period so results are comparable across reports with different date ranges[4].

h3.h3: How does the standard split internal vs external recruiting costs?

evidence.gloss: Standard separates internal vs external cost categories; this split is the backbone of credible CPH calculations
evidence.verbatim: The standard explicitly separates costs into two categories — internal (staff, capital, and organizational costs of the recruiting function) and external (payments to outside vendors or services) — and this internal/external split is the backbone of every credible cost-per-hire calculation[9][23].

evidence.gloss: Standard splits recruiting spend into internal and external categories
evidence.verbatim: The standard splits recruiting spend into two categories so organizations can see which activities drive their spend[18][3]:

evidence.gloss: List of internal cost items
evidence.verbatim: **Internal costs**: fully loaded compensation (salary plus benefits) for the talent-acquisition team and recruiters, sourcing-staff time, internal referral-program administration, recruiter training and development, recruiting-department overhead and infrastructure, recruiting technology/ATS subscriptions, compliance and administrative overhead, and internal recruitment costs for the recruiting team[18][3][17].

evidence.gloss: List of external cost items
evidence.verbatim: **External costs**: job advertising and job-board posting fees, third-party recruiter/agency/search-firm fees, job fairs and campus recruiting, signing bonuses, candidate travel reimbursement, background checks and drug screening, relocation packages, employee referral rewards, and recruiting-technology or ATS subscriptions attributable to external spend[18][13][15][3].

evidence.gloss: SHRM/ANSI standard delineates internal vs external cost components
evidence.verbatim: The SHRM/ANSI standard "explicitly delineates internal vs. external cost components," covering recruiting staff salaries and benefits (fully loaded cost), prorated hiring-manager interview time, recruiting department overhead (office infrastructure share, compliance costs), and internal sourcing costs[17].

h3.h3: What quality and transparency practices does the standard require?

evidence.gloss: Standard requires quality/transparency actions like a representative sample
evidence.verbatim: The standard describes the specific actions required to calculate cost-per-hire "to maintain quality and transparency, including creating a representative sample"[9].

evidence.gloss: Standard specifies required actions for quality/transparency including representative sample
evidence.verbatim: The Standard also specifies what actions must be taken when calculating cost-per-hire "to maintain quality and transparency, including creating a representative" sample of hires[4].

evidence.gloss: Hiring managers' interview/screening time proration is optional and only if a specific reason exists
evidence.verbatim: Some organizations also prorate hiring managers' interview and screening time into this bucket, though sources note this "isn't necessary and might make calculations difficult" and should be included "only if you have a specific reason"[15].

h3.h3: Why does CPH still vary in practice despite the standard?

evidence.gloss: Scope of included costs still varies by organization
evidence.verbatim: Even so, the scope of included costs can vary slightly by organization or context, and not every company implements the standard in exactly the same way[1].

evidence.gloss: Standard allows discretionary exclusion of ambiguous costs, with disclosure
evidence.verbatim: The standard itself builds in a discretionary allowance: for costs that are ambiguous — for example, assisting a candidate with a house purchase — the compiler calculating CPH has the discretion to exclude the expense from the report, but must explicitly note the exclusion[9].

evidence.gloss: Not every company implements the standard the same way
evidence.verbatim: "not every company implements it in exactly the same way. For example, some HR departments might exclude certain indirect costs (like hiring managers' time) for simplicity, while others might include additional items (some include onboarding costs in CPH, though this is not standard)"[17]

evidence.gloss: Importance of documenting CPH calculation method for apples-to-apples comparison
evidence.verbatim: the source stresses it is "important for organizations to document their CPH calculation method so that comparisons are apples-to-apples"[17]

evidence.gloss: A third source flags that the SHRM/ANSI standard is widely adopted but applied inconsistently in practice
evidence.verbatim: A third source addresses the standardization gap directly, noting that while the SHRM/ANSI standard has "gone a long way toward establishing a common approach" and most large organizations adhere to it or a close variant, implementation is inconsistent in practice

evidence.gloss: Examples of inconsistent practice: some exclude hiring-manager time, others include onboarding costs
evidence.verbatim: some HR departments exclude indirect costs like hiring managers' time for simplicity, while others include onboarding costs in CPH despite this not being standard practice[17].

evidence.gloss: That source recommends documenting the calculation method for apples-to-apples comparison
evidence.verbatim: This source explicitly recommends that organizations document their calculation method so comparisons remain "apples-to-apples,"

evidence.gloss: That source also breaks down how CPH's meaning shifts across corporate, agency, and contingent hiring models
evidence.verbatim: and it further breaks down how the metric's meaning shifts across corporate (in-house), agency, and contingent hiring models[17].

evidence.verbatim: a related, more restrictive Cost-per-Hire Comparable (CPHC) formula uses a defined set of 35 line items so that figures can be compared apples-to-apples across organizations[4].

evidence.gloss: CPHC comparable formula uses 35 line items for cross-org comparison
evidence.verbatim: a related comparable formula (CPHC) uses a more restrictive set of 35 line items specifically designed for cross-organization comparison[4]

h3.h3: How do you apply the standard with a calculator and worked example?

evidence.gloss: ANSI/SHRM framework applied to pinpoint spend and build a defensible budget
evidence.verbatim: Organizations apply the standardized ANSI/SHRM cost-per-hire components to "pinpoint exactly where recruitment dollars are being spent, identify opportunities to reduce costs without sacrificing hire quality, and build a transparent, defensible recruitment budget that supports strategic workforce planning"[15].

evidence.gloss: Advanced-option ANSI/SHRM components list
evidence.verbatim: Advanced-option components applied within this framework include relocation fees, candidate travel expense reimbursement, job fair and recruiting event costs, and average first-year salary,

evidence.gloss: Average first-year salary used to calculate the Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR)
evidence.verbatim: the last of which is used to calculate the Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR) — recruitment spend expressed as a percentage of total first-year compensation[15].

evidence.gloss: Worked example of internal cost components totaling $308,500
evidence.verbatim: A worked example illustrates how gathered internal costs feed the calculation: recruitment team compensation packages ($250,000), overhead and administrative fees ($25,000), training and development costs ($5,000), employee referrals ($13,000), a company-sponsored networking event ($500), and a candidate relationship management subscription ($15,000), totaling $308,500 in internal recruiting costs for the year[14].

evidence.gloss: Total hires definition and final applied CPH calculation
evidence.verbatim: This total is then combined with external costs and divided by total hires (defined as all employees brought into the organization in the period, regardless of department, role, level, or location, and optionally including contingent workers such as independent contractors, freelancers, gig workers, or consultants) to produce the applied CPH figure[14].

evidence.gloss: ANSI/SHRM calculator input model overview
evidence.verbatim: The most common calculator format organizes inputs into a small number of fixed categories that map directly onto the ANSI/SHRM 08001.2012 cost-per-hire standard[4].

evidence.gloss: General settings inputs (currency, reporting period, total hires)
evidence.verbatim: **1. General settings** — Currency (a choice of roughly 15 global currencies: USD, EUR, GBP, INR, and more), Reporting Period (Annual, Semi-Annual, Quarterly, or Monthly, with HR salaries automatically prorated to the selected period), and Total Hires (the number of positions filled in the period, used as the divisor in the formula)[1].

evidence.gloss: Internal recruitment cost inputs
evidence.verbatim: **2. Internal recruitment costs** — HR/Recruiting Staff Salaries (annual compensation for in-house recruiters, prorated to the reporting period), Employee Referral Awards (bonuses for successful referrals), Interview Expenses (interviewer time and materials), and Signing Bonuses (one-time payments to new hires)[1].

evidence.gloss: External recruitment cost inputs
evidence.verbatim: **3. External recruitment costs** — Job Board/Advertising Fees (job postings and paid ad channels), Recruitment Agency Fees (external staffing agency or headhunter fees), ATS/Technology Costs (applicant tracking system subscription and licensing fees), and Background Checks/Drug Testing (pre-employment screening and verification)[1].

evidence.gloss: Advanced option inputs incl. RCR unlock
evidence.verbatim: **4. Advanced options** — Relocation Fees, Travel Expenses (Candidates, i.e., interview-process travel reimbursements), Job Fairs/Recruiting Events, and Average First-Year Salary, which unlocks a Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR) calculation[1].

evidence.gloss: Recruiting Cost Ratio formula and its condition
evidence.verbatim: Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR) = (Total Recruitment Costs / (Average First-Year Salary × Total Hires)) × 100 — available only when Average First-Year Salary is supplied[1]

evidence.gloss: CPH framework offers Brief and Detailed versions, mapped to ANSI/SHRM standard
evidence.verbatim: One cost-per-hire framework offers both a "Brief" version (a streamlined worksheet completable in under an hour) and a "Detailed" version (a comprehensive analysis and optimization guide), with templates carrying customizable line items that are explicitly mapped to the ANSI/SHRM standard framework[8].

evidence.gloss: That tool segments CPH by department/role/location/channel and adds benchmarking guidance
evidence.verbatim: This tool goes beyond simple cost entry: it segments cost per hire by department, role level, geographic location, and source channel, and pairs the calculation with benchmarking guidance drawn from SHRM, Mercer, and CUPA-HR data[8].

evidence.gloss: Checklist extends into optimization strategy, cost tracking system design, and formal benchmarking sources with published medians
evidence.verbatim: Its accompanying checklist format extends into optimization strategy (channel-mix analysis, agency fee renegotiation, employer-brand investment to reduce paid sourcing dependency), data collection and tracking design (integrating cost tracking into the ATS, procurement system, and general ledger via standardized cost codes, with monthly reconciliation and requisition-level cost tracking), and formal benchmarking against the SHRM annual Human Capital Benchmarking Report, the CIPD Resourcing and Talent Planning Survey, and consultancy data from Bersin, PwC Saratoga, and Mercer, with published medians cited at roughly £3,000–£5,000 for professional roles and higher for executive searches[8].

evidence.verbatim: External costs are payments made to outside vendors or individuals during recruiting — job advertising and job board fees, third-party recruiting/agency fees, background checks, referral rewards, and recruiting technology or ATS subscription costs[3].

evidence.verbatim: Internal costs include recruiting staff salaries and benefits (fully loaded compensation for in-house recruiters, talent acquisition team members, and coordinators, including prorated time from HR staff or hiring managers spent interviewing or recruiting), and recruiting department overhead such as a share of office rent, utilities, and equipment allocated to recruiting activities[1].

sections.h2: How Do You Calculate Cost per Hire? Rules and Worked Examples

h3.h3: The rules for counting hires and costs correctly

evidence.gloss: Denominator counts hires who accepted offers and started, not offers extended
evidence.verbatim: The denominator counts employees who accepted offers **and started** during the measurement period — not offers extended[23][11].

evidence.gloss: Rule: match the cost period to the hire period
evidence.verbatim: match the cost period to the hire period (don't compare annual costs against monthly or quarterly hires)

evidence.gloss: Rule: count whole hires, not fractional full-time-equivalents
evidence.verbatim: count whole hires rather than fractional full-time-equivalents[6].

evidence.gloss: Counting offers instead of starts artificially deflates the metric since a declined offer is 100% cost, 0% return
evidence.verbatim: Counting offers instead of starts artificially deflates the metric, and this matters because a declined offer represents 100% of the cost with 0% of the return

h3.h3: Recruiting Cost Ratio: an alternative metric

evidence.gloss: Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR) variant differs in denominator
evidence.verbatim: A related variant is the Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR), which varies from the CPHI or CPHC formulas only in its denominator: instead of dividing by number of hires, the RCR divides total recruiting costs by the total first-year annual compensation of the new hires[9].

evidence.gloss: RCR produces a ratio, not a flat dollar figure
evidence.verbatim: This produces a ratio (cost as a percentage of first-year pay) rather than a flat dollar figure per hire.

h3.h3: Simple worked examples across company sizes

evidence.gloss: Worked example: 40-person company, 8 roles, $15,000 total = $1,875 per hire
evidence.verbatim: A 40-person company filling 8 roles in a quarter: $6,000 external (job board posts, background checks, one contingency agency fee) + $9,000 internal (hiring manager and recruiter time) = $15,000 ÷ 8 hires = **$1,875 per hire**[6].

evidence.gloss: Worked example: mid-size company, $250,000 total ÷ 25 hires = $10,000 per hire (hire count inconsistency noted)
evidence.verbatim: A mid-size company with 10 hires, $150,000 internal and $100,000 external costs: $250,000 ÷ 25 hires = **$10,000 per hire** (note: example states 25 hires elsewhere in the same source)[15].

evidence.gloss: Worked example: 200-person company, 40 hires - internal costs breakdown totaling $70,000
evidence.verbatim: A 200-person company with 40 hires: internal costs of recruiter salary allocation ($48,000) + hiring manager time ($12,000) + HR admin ($6,000) + prorated ATS ($4,000) = $70,000

evidence.gloss: Worked example: 200-person company external costs breakdown $50,000, total $3,000 per hire
evidence.verbatim: external costs of job boards ($18,000) + two agency placements ($22,000) + background checks ($4,000) + referral bonuses ($6,000) = $50,000. Total $120,000 ÷ 40 hires = **$3,000 per hire**[11].

evidence.gloss: Worked example: two-month period, 3 hires - internal costs itemized totaling $26,080
evidence.verbatim: A two-month hiring period yielding 3 hires: internal costs totaling $26,080 (HR salary $20,000, ATS $50, background software $50, recruitment software $50, job board fees $30, job fair $150, travel to job fair $500, onboarding $2,250 at 10 hours × 3 employees × $75/hour, and productivity loss of $3,000 at 30 hours × $100/hour)

evidence.gloss: Worked example: two-month period external costs $1,200 itemized, total $9,093.33 per hire
evidence.verbatim: plus external costs of $1,200 (agency fees $500, travel to job fair $500, legal fees $200) = $27,280 ÷ 3 hires = **$9,093.33 per hire**[24].

evidence.gloss: Worked example: hypothetical 50-hire year, $100,000 total spend = $2,000 per hire
evidence.verbatim: A hypothetical 50-hire year with $100,000 total spend yields **$2,000 per hire**[23].

evidence.gloss: Worked example: $150k internal + $100k external / 25 hires = $10k CPH
evidence.verbatim: A worked example from this calculator: total internal costs of $150,000 plus total external costs of $100,000 across 25 hires yields a cost-per-hire of $10,000[5] (a separate source citing the same style of calculation independently confirms this input/output shape).

evidence.gloss: Worked example: small-company CPH calculation ($1,875)
evidence.verbatim: Illustrative benchmark math from an SHRM-adjacent source: a 40-person company filling 8 roles in a quarter, with external costs of $6,000 (job board posts, background checks, one contingency agency fee) and internal costs of $9,000 (hiring manager and recruiter time), yields ($6,000 + $9,000) ÷ 8 = $1,875 per hire — well below the SHRM average, attributed to smaller companies not filling executive or specialized technical roles at the same rate as large enterprises[5].

evidence.gloss: Worked scenario: two-recruiter Corporate team CPH, seat cost vs with recruiter time added
evidence.verbatim: a two-recruiter team on Corporate seats at $10,800/year each, making 40 hires annually, pays approximately $540 per hire in seat costs alone, rising to $1,600–$2,000+ once 15–20 hours of recruiter time per hire is added;

evidence.gloss: Worked scenario: solo recruiter Lite tier CPH vs larger team's labor cost
evidence.verbatim: a solo recruiter on the Lite tier making 6 hires per year pays $280 per hire in seat costs, with the same per-hire labor cost as the larger team[28].

evidence.gloss: Mid-level hiring loop direct cost: $4,000-$8,000
evidence.verbatim: a typical mid-level hiring loop runs $4,000-$8,000 in direct cost

evidence.gloss: Engineering loop with full onsite panel: $6,000-$23,000
evidence.verbatim: an engineering loop with a full onsite panel runs $6,000-$23,000

h3.h3: Detailed itemized cost breakdowns (international examples)

evidence.gloss: Worked example: itemized indirect cost for a European sales hire (€7,966)
evidence.verbatim: It provides an itemized worked example for a sales hire in Europe: interview and screening hours (6 hrs at €45/hr = €270; 4 hrs hiring-manager interviews at €45/hr = €180; 4 hrs second-round panel at €38/hr avg = €152; 2 hrs reference calls at €22/hr = €44; 3 hrs HR admin at €28/hr = €84), plus 38 days of role-open coverage cost at €180/day = €6,840, for a total indirect cost of €7,966[11].

evidence.gloss: Same example's post-hire cost breakdown (€5,730 total)
evidence.verbatim: Post-hire costs in the same example: €400 onboarding, €250 sales tools training, €1,080 manager coaching (8 hrs/month × 3 months × €45/hr), and €4,000 productivity ramp gap (4 months × €2,500/month × 40% average gap), totaling €5,730[11].

evidence.gloss: Combined total CPH for the example: €14,451 (48% of base salary)
evidence.verbatim: Combined, this yields a total cost-per-hire of €14,451 — 48% of the role's annual base salary[11].

evidence.gloss: Second worked example: mid-market senior software engineer hire via agency (Germany)
evidence.verbatim: A second worked example (mid-market senior software engineer hire via agency, Germany, €90,000 base) itemizes an 18% agency fee of €16,200, an €85 background check, and a technical assessment platform fee[11].

evidence.gloss: Engineer-hire scenario: direct costs breakdown totaling €17,005
evidence.verbatim: One detailed scenario for hiring an engineer breaks out direct costs (including a €280 ATS cost attribution and €320 candidate travel line, totaling €17,005)

evidence.gloss: Engineer-hire scenario: indirect costs breakdown totaling €24,864
evidence.verbatim: indirect costs (hiring manager briefing and shortlist review hours at €65/hr, technical interview rounds across three engineers at an average €58/hr, and a productivity gap of €450/day over a 52-day open role, totaling €24,864)

evidence.gloss: Engineer-hire scenario: post-hire costs breakdown totaling €20,350
evidence.verbatim: and post-hire costs (onboarding and developer environment setup at €800, a formal technical onboarding program at €1,200, mentoring hours, and a ramp-period productivity gap, totaling €20,350)

evidence.gloss: Engineer-hire scenario total: €62,219 CPH, 69% of annual salary / ~7 months to full productivity
evidence.verbatim: yielding a total cost-per-hire of €62,219, equivalent to 69% of annual base salary or nearly seven months of salary before the engineer reaches full productivity[11].

sections.h2: How Do Cost-Per-Hire Calculators Work, and What Do They Miss?

target_keyword.why: Directly matches the section's subject and carries zero difficulty against decent volume.

h3.h3: What a CPH Calculator Actually Calculates

evidence.gloss: Definition and naming of Cost-Per-Hire calculators
evidence.verbatim: Dedicated Cost-Per-Hire Calculators — also referred to as Recruitment Cost Calculators or Hiring Cost Calculators — are workforce analytics tools built around the ANSI/SHRM standard formula[15].

evidence.gloss: Two input categories the calculators accept
evidence.verbatim: They typically accept a wide range of inputs across two categories: internal recruitment costs (such as annual salary data prorated to a selected period) and external recruitment costs[15].

evidence.gloss: Calculators compute recruiting cost ratio as % of first-year comp
evidence.verbatim: calculate recruiting cost ratios as a percentage of first-year compensation[15].

evidence.gloss: Core data inputs a CPH tool must aggregate
evidence.verbatim: the underlying data a CPH tool needs to pull together includes vendor invoices, recruiting software subscriptions, and internal time estimates for recruiters and hiring managers

evidence.gloss: Some inputs are exact, others are estimates; SHRM wants high quality not penny-precision
evidence.verbatim: some inputs (agency invoices) are exact while others (recruiter salary allocation) are necessarily estimates — the SHRM standard calls for high data quality, not penny-by-penny reconciliation[6].

evidence.gloss: CPH tools typology framing: connected vs standalone to taxonomy/standard/benchmarks
evidence.verbatim: The collected material shows cost-per-hire (CPH) tools clustering into a few distinct types, distinguished mainly by whether the line items they surface are left to stand alone or are explicitly tied back to a documented cost taxonomy, a named standard, and benchmark data the user is told how to apply.

h3.h3: Calculator Examples: iCIMS, Connecteam, and Generic Tools

evidence.gloss: iCIMS Cost-Per-Hire Report example
evidence.verbatim: iCIMS' Applicant Tracking platform is cited as an example: its Cost-Per-Hire Report automatically calculates and segments CPH

evidence.gloss: iCIMS Expense Tracking feature
evidence.verbatim: its Expense Tracking feature allows internal and external recruitment costs (job board postings, travel expenses, etc.) to be added directly to a job profile for a holistic view of recruitment spend in one place[14].

evidence.gloss: Channel-level cost tracking is a distinct software function
evidence.verbatim: Because not every sourcing channel produces hires at the same cost, tracking cost per hire by channel — job boards, referrals, agencies, talent communities, career site traffic, and outbound sourcing — is treated as a distinct software function[6].

evidence.gloss: Connecteam's simplified comparable calculator structure
evidence.verbatim: A second, similarly-scoped tool (Connecteam's free calculator) uses a comparable but simplified structure: total hires and average hours spent per hire as basic info; internal costs limited to HR salaries, referral awards, signing bonuses, and interview costs; and external costs limited to job board fees, ATS fees, background checks, drug testing, and "other external fees"[2].

evidence.gloss: Connecteam's enter-basics → add-internal → add-external → calculate flow
evidence.verbatim: It explicitly follows the same enter-basics → add-internal → add-external → calculate flow[2].

evidence.gloss: Third source's simplified SHRM formula and core line items
evidence.verbatim: A third source describes the SHRM cost-per-hire formula in its simplest form as total external costs plus total internal costs, divided by hires, and lists the same core line items: third-party agency fees, advertising agency fees, job fairs, and (implicitly) internal staff cost[5][21].

evidence.gloss: Connecteam's calculator is comparatively self-contained, less benchmark-dense
evidence.verbatim: Connecteam's calculator is comparatively self-contained: it names the SHRM formula it uses but its own page content is largely limited to describing the tool's four steps and defining cost-per-hire as "total expenses associated with recruiting a new employee, divided by the number of hires," without the same density of external benchmark citation seen in the other two[2].

evidence.gloss: Generic calculator breaks costs into named internal vs external categories
evidence.verbatim: Breaking internal vs. external cost inputs into named categories (HR/recruiting staff salaries prorated to a reporting period, employee referral awards, interview expenses, signing bonuses on the internal side; job board/advertising fees and other line items on the external side)[1].

evidence.gloss: Generic calculator computes a secondary Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR) metric
evidence.verbatim: Computing a secondary ratio, the Recruiting Cost Ratio (RCR) = (Total Recruitment Costs / (Average First-Year Salary × Total Hires)) × 100, when average first-year salary is supplied[1].

evidence.gloss: Generic calculator's external benchmark figures: ~$4,700 average, $14,000+ for executives
evidence.verbatim: Citing external benchmark figures for context: ~$4,700 average cost-per-hire across industries, and executive/C-suite hires exceeding $14,000

evidence.gloss: Sector-level cost notes: healthcare/tech above average, retail/hospitality below median
evidence.verbatim: with sector-level notes that healthcare and technology (specialized skills) report higher-than-average costs while retail and hospitality (higher volume, lower specialization) fall below the median[1].

evidence.gloss: Generic calculator pairs number with five prescriptive cost-reduction levers
evidence.verbatim: Pairing the calculator with prescriptive guidance rather than leaving the number to stand alone: five named levers to reduce cost-per-hire without cutting quality (build a referral program, since referred hires cost 40-60% less than agency placements and retain better; audit job board spend-to-hire ratios; reduce agency dependency via internal sourcing/talent pools; reallocate budget toward better-performing channels; strengthen employer branding to reduce paid-channel dependence)[16][1].

evidence.gloss: Generic calculator's FAQ ties cost-per-hire to budget justification
evidence.verbatim: Answering an FAQ ("Why does cost per hire matter?") that ties the metric back to budget justification and hiring-investment alignment rather than presenting it as an isolated output[1].

evidence.gloss: Interview cost calculator uses a five-component model and invites SHRM benchmark comparison
evidence.verbatim: A separate interview cost calculator applies what it calls "the full five-component model" (direct interview costs plus components most simple formulas omit, such as productivity loss and cost of a mis-hire) and explicitly invites users to "compare your number against the SHRM benchmark," citing SHRM's figure as $5,475[7].

evidence.gloss: Two-recruiter Corporate team scenario: $540/hire in seat costs, up to $1,600-$2,000+ with labor time
evidence.verbatim: illustrated with two scenarios — a two-recruiter team on Corporate seats at $10,800/year each making 40 hires pays about $540/hire in seat costs alone, climbing to $1,600-$2,000+ once 15-20 hours of recruiter time per hire is added;

evidence.gloss: Solo recruiter Lite scenario: $280/hire in seat costs plus same labor cost
evidence.verbatim: a solo recruiter on Lite making 6 hires/year pays $280/hire in seat costs but carries the same per-hire labor cost[28].

evidence.gloss: Truffle: resume screening/interview/assessment platform, $49/month credit-based, 7-day trial, ~10-min setup
evidence.verbatim: Truffle is described as a resume-screening, one-way video interview, and assessment platform, credit-based from $49/month with a 7-day free trial and roughly 10-minute setup, framed purely as a way to process applications faster ("Indeed brings you applicants. Truffle helps you get through them fast")[10].

h3.h3: What Drives Cost-Per-Hire Up or Down

evidence.gloss: Automation reports up to 30% cost reduction
evidence.verbatim: Companies that implement recruitment automation report cost reductions of up to 30% while also improving candidate experience and reducing time-to-fill[15].

evidence.gloss: AI-flagged consistency and scorecards reduce mis-hire variance
evidence.verbatim: AI-flagged interview consistency is cited as a mechanism, alongside structured scorecards, for reducing the variance that produces mis-hires

evidence.gloss: Mis-hires are excluded from standard CPH and cost 1-2x salary, recognized later
evidence.verbatim: which the source notes are typically excluded from standard CPH calculations because a mis-hire (costing 1–2 times annual salary in re-fill, ramp-down, and ramp-up) is recognized in a later quarter than the one in which the hire was made[27].

evidence.gloss: Time-to-hire is the hardest CPH input to track accurately
evidence.verbatim: Time-to-hire is described as the most difficult cost-per-hire input to track accurately, since most calculators simply subtract the posting date from the hire date and ignore screening and coordination time[6].

evidence.gloss: Dedicated time-to-hire calculator example with €100/hour math
evidence.verbatim: A dedicated time-to-hire and screening-efficiency calculator is referenced as a way to capture average hours per candidate more precisely — for example, a team averaging 10 hours total per hire at €100/hour adds €1,000 to the calculation[6].

evidence.gloss: Async video interview tools reduce live-coordination cost burden
evidence.verbatim: Async video interview tools are cited as a way to make candidate responses available for review and to score candidates using a built-in scorecard feature, reducing the internal-cost burden of live interview coordination[21].

h3.h3: Adjacent Tool Costs CPH Calculators Don't Capture

evidence.gloss: ATS pricing comparison: per-user/month ranges and feature tags across 6 platforms
evidence.verbatim: The ATS pricing comparison surveying 30+ platforms is the clearest example: it lists per-user/month ranges (Workable $60–$150, Greenhouse $80+, Lever $70–$200, SmartRecruiters $50–$150, JazzHR $30–$100, Breezy HR $40–$130) alongside feature tags like "pipeline management" or "candidate scoring,"

evidence.gloss: ATS pricing variance stat: average ~$80/user/month but real range $15–$300+
evidence.verbatim: The piece does note that ATS pricing is "all over the map" ($50–$150/user/month for full-featured plans, ~$80 average, but real costs swinging from ~$15 to $300+ depending on per-user/per-job/usage billing)

evidence.gloss: ATS implementation cost range $5,000–$100,000+, still framed as standalone purchase not CPH input
evidence.verbatim: and that implementation can range from trivial for small teams to $5,000–$100,000+ once data migration, custom workflows, integrations, and paid training are added, yet this is framed as a standalone purchasing decision, not as an input plugged into a documented CPH pillar[9].

evidence.gloss: Indeed/LinkedIn comparison: pricing, $25/day sponsorship floor since July 2025, framed only as channel-selection guide
evidence.verbatim: The Indeed/LinkedIn comparison presents quote-based Recruiter and job-posting pricing, the $25/day per-posting sponsorship floor in effect since July 2025, and decision heuristics ("are you short on applications, or buried in them?") purely as a channel-selection guide, without referencing back to a cost-per-hire calculation or a hard/soft cost taxonomy[10].

evidence.gloss: Sourcing-tool tier comparison (InMail credits, 28+ ATS integrations, data ownership) presented as feature matrix, not CPH-linked
evidence.verbatim: Similarly, the Corporate/Lite/Professional sourcing-tool tier comparison (InMail credit allocations, integration with 28+ ATS platforms including Greenhouse, Workable, and Lever, and the data-ownership distinction between individual-recruiter-owned versus organization-owned candidate data) is presented as a feature/tier decision matrix, with no line drawn to how these subscription costs should be allocated into a CPH figure[28].

h3.h3: The Methodological Gap: Why a Simple Number Isn't Enough

evidence.gloss: Cost-per-hire calculators focus on the easiest-to-itemize costs, not what actually drives total cost
evidence.verbatim: Standalone cost-per-hire calculators are frequently built around what is easiest to itemize — job ad spend, recruiter fees, background checks, onboarding line items — rather than what actually drives the total cost of a hire.

evidence.gloss: This mirrors the direct-cost vs indirect-cost distinction (visible/easy vs hidden/impactful)
evidence.verbatim: This split mirrors the direct-cost/indirect-cost distinction: direct costs are "visible, often tangible... relatively easy to measure and control," while indirect costs are "hidden... but equally impactful," including lost productivity, knowledge gaps left by departing employees, and disruption to teams while a role sits open[29].

evidence.gloss: A calculator that only counts ad spend and agency fees captures only the easy half of the number
evidence.verbatim: A calculator that only asks for ad spend and agency fees is, by definition, capturing the easy half of the number.

evidence.gloss: There is a methodological gap between what a simple calculator does and rigorous cost-allocation practice
evidence.verbatim: There is also a methodological gap between what a simple calculator does and what a rigorous cost-allocation exercise requires.

evidence.gloss: Rigorous cost allocation requires activity-based costing, documented rules, sensitivity analysis, requisition-level tracking, and monthly reconciliation
evidence.verbatim: Recommended practice calls for allocating shared costs (recruiter salaries, employer branding spend, corporate overhead) using activity-based costing "where feasible," documenting allocation rules and applying them consistently across periods, and explicitly acknowledging "that some allocation methods involve judgement" via sensitivity analysis — alongside building requisition-level cost tracking with standardized cost codes tied into the ATS and general ledger, and running a monthly reconciliation process "to ensure recruitment spending is fully captured"[8].

evidence.gloss: A one-time standalone calculator has no mechanism for ongoing reconciliation or showing its allocation assumptions
evidence.verbatim: A one-time, standalone calculator that outputs a single blended number has no mechanism for this ongoing reconciliation or for showing its allocation assumptions.

evidence.gloss: Different stakeholders (HR, Finance, Recruiting) apply the same CPH/vacancy figure differently
evidence.verbatim: The same limitation shows up at the stakeholder level: the "tactical calculation" behind a vacancy or CPH figure is OPEX savings and revenue/production loss per seat, but different stakeholders apply it differently — HR leaders factor in onboarding, training, and cultural impact; Finance factors in ramp, revenue, and commission; Recruiting leaders treat backfill requests as unplanned demand on capacity[32].

evidence.gloss: A single flat calculator output can't serve all stakeholder audiences and gives no guidance on why a number is high or how to fix it
evidence.verbatim: A single flat calculator output, disconnected from a broader framework, cannot serve all three audiences at once, and by itself gives no guidance on "why" a number is high or how to fix it, which is presented as the actual point of the exercise: "Both parties will want to know WHY and have a way to fix it"[32].

sections.h2: What does cost-per-hire actually benchmark to?

h3.h3: The old SHRM figures ($4,000-$4,700) and why they're dated

evidence.gloss: Most-cited CPH benchmark: SHRM $4,129
evidence.verbatim: The most frequently cited benchmark traces back to SHRM's Human Capital Benchmarking Report, which found an average U.S. cost per hire of $4,129[3].

evidence.gloss: $4,129 figure still cited despite age
evidence.verbatim: Despite its age, this number is still widely cited in publications as a current reference point, even though it should be treated as historical context rather than a target to chase[6][3].

evidence.gloss: Secondary sources citing ~$4,700 average
evidence.verbatim: Other secondary sources citing SHRM data give a figure of "nearly $4,700" as the average cost per hire[20][21], with some noting executive or highly specialized roles can soar to $28,000 or more[21].

evidence.gloss: 2015-era $4,000 estimate
evidence.verbatim: A separate 2015-era estimate placed the average cost per hire by U.S. industries at $4,000[22].

evidence.gloss: Origin and dated nature of the SHRM $4,129 average CPH figure
evidence.verbatim: The often-cited SHRM figure of $4,129 average cost per hire comes from the 2016 Human Capital Benchmarking Report, using fiscal year 2015 data collected from 2,048 SHRM members (average time to fill in the same report was 42 days)[3].

evidence.gloss: SHRM survey average US CPH $4,000-$4,700
evidence.verbatim: SHRM survey data places the average U.S. cost per hire at roughly $4,000–$4,700[17]

evidence.gloss: Separate reference gives $4,000 as 2015 US average
evidence.verbatim: while a separate reference gives $4,000 as the 2015 U.S. industry average[15].

evidence.gloss: UK CIPD average CPH figure
evidence.verbatim: UK data from the CIPD (Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development) puts the average at approximately £6,125 per hire when internal staff time and external fees are both factored in[17].

evidence.gloss: April 2022 SHRM figure of nearly $4,700
evidence.verbatim: A later SHRM publication, "The Real Costs of Recruitment" (April 2022), reported the figure at "nearly $4,700"[7].

evidence.gloss: SHRM average CPH figure $4,700
evidence.verbatim: the canonical SHRM figure of average cost-per-hire at $4,700

evidence.gloss: Framework restates SHRM benchmark ~$4,700
evidence.verbatim: this source also restates the SHRM benchmark ("approximately $4,700")

evidence.gloss: ANSI/SHRM calculator's cited benchmark: ~$4,700 avg CPH, $14,000+ for executives, varies by industry/geography
evidence.verbatim: The ANSI/SHRM-style calculator explicitly cites its benchmark context: SHRM data puts average cost-per-hire across all industries at approximately $4,700, with executive/C-suite roles routinely exceeding $14,000, and states these figures vary by industry, role complexity, geography, and labor-market conditions, with healthcare and technology skewing higher and retail/hospitality skewing lower[1].

h3.h3: SHRM's 2025 benchmark update

evidence.gloss: SHRM 2025 benchmark figures
evidence.verbatim: The SHRM 2025 Benchmarking Report puts average cost per hire at $5,475 for all industries in non-executive roles, and $35,879 for executive roles[6].

evidence.gloss: SHRM 2025 Benchmarking Survey methodology and sample
evidence.verbatim: The headline figures most organizations benchmark against come from SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Survey, fielded electronically among a random sample of active SHRM members between January 9 and March 3, 2025, with 2,371 respondents and a stratified oversample of vice-president-or-higher roles[12].

evidence.gloss: SHRM 2025 benchmarking: executive hires ~7x more expensive
evidence.verbatim: SHRM's 2025 benchmarking reports (88 individual data sets spanning industry, sector, organization size, and region) found that executive hires are, on average, nearly 7x more expensive than nonexecutive hires[6]

evidence.gloss: Updated SHRM 2025 benchmark: $5,475 non-executive / $35,879 executive, 21% jump from 2022
evidence.verbatim: A separate SHRM-benchmark citation (from a different vendor's article) updates this figure: SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report puts the U.S. average at $5,475 per hire for non-executive roles and $35,879 for executive roles — a 21% jump from 2022 — while noting the older $4,700 figure is still commonly seen[5].

evidence.gloss: Description of SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report scope and release date
evidence.verbatim: The most current figures come from SHRM's 2025 Benchmarking Report (released October 15, 2025, covering CHRO Metrics, Learning and Development, Recruiting, and Talent Management across 88 individual data sets segmented by industry, sector, organization size, and region)[6][7].

evidence.gloss: 2025 national average CPH: non-executive vs executive
evidence.verbatim: That report puts the national average cost per hire at $5,475 for all-industry, non-executive hires, and $35,879 for executive roles — nearly 7x the non-executive figure[6][5][7].

evidence.gloss: SHRM's 2025 benchmarking research scope: 88 data sets from its Benchmarking Database
evidence.verbatim: SHRM also backs the calculator with ongoing benchmarking research: the 2025 benchmarking release covers 88 individual data sets spanning overall figures, industry groupings, sectors, organization sizes, and regions, drawn from SHRM's Benchmarking Database of a random sample of SHRM member organizations[6][24].

evidence.gloss: SHRM non-executive cost-per-hire figures: $4,700 to $5,475 (21% jump)
evidence.verbatim: That research reports non-executive cost-per-hire at roughly $4,700 in the older figure, updated to $5,475 in the 2025 report (a 21% jump from 2022)

evidence.gloss: SHRM executive cost-per-hire: $35,879, ~7x non-executive
evidence.verbatim: with executive hires averaging $35,879 — nearly 7x more expensive than nonexecutive hires[6][5][11].

h3.h3: How to actually use a CPH benchmark

evidence.gloss: The SHRM number is a moving target, not stable
evidence.verbatim: These varying figures illustrate how the "SHRM number" circulating in the industry is not a single stable data point but a moving target that has shifted across benchmarking cycles.

evidence.gloss: $4,700 vs $7,000 CPH gap framed as more than an accounting detail; CPH rising ~14% periodically
evidence.verbatim: One industry source frames the gap starkly: the difference between a reported $4,700 and a fuller $7,000 per hire is described as "more than an accounting detail" — it is the difference between sustainable growth and a looming budget crisis, and CPH has reportedly risen roughly 14% every few years as this gap widens[7].

evidence.gloss: SHRM benchmark should be historical context, not a current target
evidence.verbatim: Critics note this should be treated as historical context, not a current target, given how dated the underlying data is[3].

evidence.gloss: Track your own CPH trend rather than relying on cross-industry benchmarks
evidence.verbatim: More broadly, CPH varies significantly by industry, role seniority, and company, so a single national or cross-industry benchmark is less useful than tracking an organization's own CPH trend over time[3].

h3.h3: Other recruiting cost and time benchmarks

evidence.gloss: Gem 2026 benchmarks: 0.5% offer rate, ~200 applications per hire, 93% YoY workload rise
evidence.verbatim: Gem's 2026 Recruiting Benchmarks Report found that only 0.5% of applicants receive an offer, meaning recruiters process roughly 200 applications per hire, and recruiter workloads climbed 93% year-over-year[10]

evidence.gloss: Recruiting budget averages 26% of total HR budget
evidence.verbatim: and that recruiting budget averages 26% of total HR budget[6].

evidence.gloss: Screening/interviewing stages average 8-9 days each
evidence.verbatim: The same 2025 reports found screening and interviewing stages alone average 8–9 days each in the job-posting-to-offer-acceptance process[6].

evidence.gloss: Background-check cost range and legal constraints

evidence.verbatim: and the sourcing technology stack itself (LinkedIn Recruiter licenses and InMail credits, Boolean search and candidate-database subscriptions)[13].

evidence.gloss: Technology/software spend is 16–18% of total recruitment budgets at larger firms, much of it redundant tool spend
evidence.verbatim: and separately notes that technology and software already account for 16–18% of total recruitment budgets at larger firms, much of it flagged as redundant spend from running separate ATS, CRM, job distribution, video interviewing, and back-office tools[30].

evidence.gloss: Same source argues assessment/video-interviewing/ATS fees are systematically underestimated as overhead, not direct hiring expense
evidence.verbatim: and separately argues that assessment platform fees, video interviewing software, and per-hire ATS allocations are systematically underestimated because they are booked as overhead rather than direct hiring expense[13].

evidence.gloss: Technology stack costs (recruiting software, licenses, subscriptions) are rarely included in CPH calculations
evidence.verbatim: "The sophisticated technology stack that powers modern recruitment is rarely included in CPH calculations," covering LinkedIn Recruiter licenses and InMail credits, Boolean search/candidate database subscriptions, assessment platform fees, video interviewing software, and per-hire ATS allocations.

evidence.gloss: Treating tech stack as overhead rather than a direct hiring expense causes CPH underestimation and distorts hiring ROI
evidence.verbatim: Because these are "treated as overheads and not direct hiring expenses, organizations underestimate the true CPH," which can "distort hiring ROI and underfund one of the most strategic levers in talent acquisition"[13].

evidence.gloss: Technology/software already makes up 16-18% of recruitment budgets at larger firms, much of it redundant across disconnected point tools
evidence.verbatim: Separately, technology and software are estimated to already account for 16–18% of total recruitment budgets at larger firms, with "a significant share of that spend... redundant" due to running five or more disconnected point tools (ATS, CRM, job distribution, video interviewing, back-office) that each carry a subscription fee, training overhead, and a data silo requiring manual re-entry[30].

h3.h3: Accounting and measurement mismatches that distort CPH

evidence.gloss: Real spend often booked as overhead rather than counted in CPH
evidence.verbatim: Several categories of real spend are frequently left out of CPH calculations entirely because they are booked as general overhead rather than direct hiring costs:

evidence.gloss: Teams often total only external vendor invoices, understating true CPH
evidence.verbatim: **Internal costs generally**: recruiter salaries, sourcing time, and recruiting overhead are real internal costs under the ANSI/SHRM standard, but many teams total only external vendor invoices (which are easier to find) and stop there, understating true CPH[3].

evidence.gloss: Mismatched cost/hire time windows make CPH meaningless
evidence.verbatim: **Mixed accounting periods**: if cost data covers one time window (e.g., a year) while hire counts cover another (e.g., a quarter), the resulting CPH figure is described as "meaningless"[3].

evidence.gloss: Blending recruiting and onboarding costs breaks benchmarking
evidence.verbatim: Similarly, blending recruiting costs with onboarding costs makes CPH impossible to benchmark against industry standards[11].

evidence.gloss: Search-fee vs. all-in-cost gap is almost never included in standard calculators
evidence.verbatim: Note: the input categories catalogued from source [1] elsewhere describe the search-fee vs. all-in-cost gap as one that "dwarfs the search fee and is almost never included in standard cost-per-hire calculations"[11], reinforcing that the component checklist itself (job ads, agency fees, ATS, background checks) is consistently the visible, invoiced portion of cost, while time-based and opportunity-cost components are the ones vendors flag as most often missing from standalone calculators[11][14].

h3.h3: Hidden costs specific to startups

evidence.gloss: Startup-focused hidden costs founders miss
evidence.verbatim: A startup-focused breakdown adds further hidden costs founders typically miss: the opportunity cost of a hiring manager's diverted attention, productivity loss during the open-role period, integration cost when a hire doesn't ramp as expected, and the cost of restarting the process after a bad hire[19].

evidence.gloss: Founder/runway framing: CPH needs runway-adjusted thinking for startups
evidence.verbatim: One source frames this explicitly as a founder/runway problem, arguing that "the percentage-based fee model was designed for organisations with stable budgets, not startups counting months," and that CPH "needs to be recalculated with runway-adjusted thinking, not just accounting-period cost"[19].

h3.h3: Offer declines as a sunk cost

evidence.gloss: 35% of candidates backed out after accepting offers in Q1 2025; a declined offer is a pure sunk cost calculators don't capture
evidence.verbatim: With 35% of candidates reported to be backing out even after accepting offers in Q1 2025, "a declined offer means you've spent the full cost of the process with zero hire to show for it" — a pure loss ("100% cost with 0% return") that a forward-looking, per-line calculator doesn't naturally account for unless offer-acceptance rate is built in as its own variable[16].

sections.h2: Is a lower cost-per-hire actually a good sign?

h3.h3: How widely is cost-per-hire tracked?

evidence.gloss: CPH remains the top-tracked HR metric per Paychex survey
evidence.verbatim: Adoption of the metric remains high despite these caveats: Paychex's 2026 Business Leaders Priorities survey found cost per hire is the number one HR metric tracked by 47% of businesses with 5 to 19 employees, and by 54% of businesses with 20 to 49 employees[6].

evidence.gloss: CPH is the most-tracked HR metric for small businesses
evidence.verbatim: CPH is the single most-tracked HR metric for 47% of businesses with 5–19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20–49 employees

h3.h3: Why do published CPH benchmarks vary so much?

evidence.gloss: Caution against treating published averages as targets
evidence.verbatim: Multiple sources caution against treating any single published average as a meaningful target.

evidence.gloss: Sources of variance in recruiting costs
evidence.verbatim: Variances in recruiting costs exist based on position type, position level, external market demand, and geographic region[9].

evidence.gloss: Caveat: benchmarks aggregate highly varied industries
evidence.verbatim: they should be applied with caution because they aggregate data across highly varied industries[23]

evidence.gloss: Caveat: role seniority/specialization drives cost
evidence.verbatim: role seniority and specialization materially drive cost (specialized or executive roles require longer sourcing cycles, more interview rounds, and greater agency/search-firm involvement, compounding internal labor cost)[26]

evidence.gloss: Caveat: company size affects per-hire cost via fixed-cost spread
evidence.verbatim: company size affects the metric because larger organizations spread fixed recruiting costs across more hires, lowering per-hire cost, while smaller teams divide the same fixed costs across fewer hires, raising it[26].

h3.h3: How a low CPH can hide poor hiring outcomes

evidence.gloss: Low CPH can mask poor hiring outcomes
evidence.verbatim: A lower cost per hire is not inherently good: it can look efficient while hiding poor outcomes if those hires leave quickly, underperform, or require the process to restart, meaning the true hiring cost is higher than the headline metric suggests[6].

evidence.gloss: a lower CPH is falsely assumed to signal efficiency
evidence.verbatim: Averages also invite a false inference: that a lower cost per hire signals efficiency. It doesn't necessarily.

evidence.gloss: a lower CPH can reflect a weak pipeline or under-investment in sourcing
evidence.verbatim: A lower CPH can just as easily reflect a weak pipeline or under-investment in sourcing rather than genuine cost discipline[8].

evidence.gloss: cutting CPH without tracking quality can raise downstream replacement hiring and total labor cost
evidence.verbatim: Reducing cost per hire without tracking quality in parallel can increase downstream replacement hiring and total labor cost

evidence.gloss: Cost reduction alone is a flawed sole objective
evidence.verbatim: This guards against treating cost reduction as the sole objective, since lower-quality hires can prove more expensive over the long term through lost productivity and higher turnover[16][7].

evidence.gloss: CPH criticized as an efficiency metric, not a quality metric
evidence.verbatim: The most persistent criticism of cost per hire (CPH) is that it measures process efficiency, not hiring quality, and treating it as a quality score is a common and costly mistake[3].

evidence.gloss: AIHR: a low CPH is not automatically good
evidence.verbatim: AIHR explicitly warns that a low cost per hire is not automatically good: it can signal sacrificed candidate quality, weaker retention, and downstream costs that don't show up in the CPH formula itself, while spending more upfront on recruiting often improves retention and long-term ROI[3].

h3.h3: Pairing CPH with quality-of-hire metrics

evidence.gloss: CPH should be tracked with complementary metrics
evidence.verbatim: Cost per hire is therefore recommended to be tracked alongside complementary metrics — time to hire, offer acceptance rate, and new-hire retention[6][22] — because on its own it reveals efficiency but not quality[22][3].

evidence.gloss: practitioners recommend a "cost per quality hire" framing pairing CPH with retention/satisfaction
evidence.verbatim: some practitioners argue for pairing CPH with a 90-day retention rate or hiring-manager satisfaction score — a "cost per quality hire" framing rather than cost in isolation[11]

evidence.gloss: only 20% of organizations track quality of hire
evidence.verbatim: This blind spot is widespread: only 20% of organizations currently track quality of hire at all[12].

evidence.gloss: Pair CPH with a quality signal rather than optimizing CPH alone
evidence.verbatim: Practitioners are advised to pair CPH with a quality signal — a 90-day retention rate or hiring manager satisfaction score — rather than optimizing CPH in isolation, since reducing cost per hire without tracking quality can increase downstream replacement hiring and total labor cost[11].

sections.h2: How do CPA and CPH reveal true sourcing-channel efficiency?

h3.h3: CPA and CPH basics: what they measure, and why cheap isn't always efficient

evidence.gloss: CPH and CPA used to compare sourcing channel efficiency
evidence.verbatim: CPH and cost-per-application (CPA) data are applied to compare channel efficiency, including job boards, referrals, agencies, talent communities, career site traffic, and outbound sourcing[6].

evidence.gloss: An expensive channel can still be efficient; a cheap one can be costly
evidence.verbatim: A channel that appears expensive upfront can still be efficient if it produces faster, higher-quality hires, while a cheap channel can prove costly if it fills the funnel with low-fit applicants that waste recruiter and manager time[6].

evidence.gloss: CPA formula definition and how it can be run
evidence.verbatim: The CPA formula itself is calculated as cost (in dollars) of posting a job listing divided by the number of job applicants, and can be run per job listing for granular data or averaged across the organization[16].

h3.h3: How CPH varies by hiring model: in-house, agency, RPO, and contingent

evidence.gloss: CPH calculations differ by hiring model
evidence.verbatim: CPH calculations are applied differently depending on the hiring model.

evidence.gloss: Agency fees inflate CPH; example of 20% fee on $100k hire
evidence.verbatim: For third-party agency recruitment, the hiring organization's CPH heavily reflects agency fees — for example, a 20% fee on a $100k hire adds $20,000 in external cost — and agencies often significantly increase CPH for senior or hard-to-fill roles[1].

evidence.gloss: RPO gives predictable fixed-fee CPH vs. contingency pay-per-hire spikes
evidence.verbatim: Recruitment process outsourcing (RPO) is noted to provide a "predictable cost-per-hire via fixed fees," in contrast to contingency agencies that operate on a pay-per-hire model that can spike costs with each hire[1].

evidence.gloss: Contingent workforce CPH based on hourly markup, not per-hire fee
evidence.verbatim: For contingent workforce hiring (temporary/contract workers via staffing firms or a Vendor Management System), cost-per-hire is defined differently and is based on an hourly markup rather than a per-hire fee[1].

evidence.gloss: Agency vs. in-house recruiter cost comparison and break-even point
evidence.verbatim: It also directly addresses whether to use an agency or in-house recruiter: agency fees run 15-25% of base salary with zero fixed cost, while an in-house recruiter at a €55,000 fully-loaded cost breaks even at roughly 8-12 mid-level hires per year[11].

evidence.gloss: Standard differentiates corporate/in-house vs contingent/contractor CPH, contractor CPH lower upfront due to agency markup
evidence.verbatim: The standard also differentiates interpretation by hiring model: corporate/in-house CPH calculation differs from contingent/contractor cost accounting, where the "cost per hire" is often lower upfront because "the agency's markup covers recruitment and is spread over time,"

evidence.gloss: Total contractor cost may still include onboarding/offboarding/conversion fees if hired full-time later
evidence.verbatim: though total cost may still include onboarding, offboarding, and conversion fees if a contractor is later hired full-time[17]

h3.h3: What inflates CPH

evidence.gloss: Sources flag mechanisms that inflate or distort CPH
evidence.verbatim: Sources also flag specific mechanisms that inflate or distort CPH if left unexamined:

evidence.gloss: Heavy agency/staffing-fee reliance is a common CPH inflator
evidence.verbatim: heavy reliance on recruiting agencies or staffing fees (a common problem when more than 30% of hires come through agencies)[11]

evidence.gloss: Job board spend with poor source-of-hire ROI
evidence.verbatim: job board spend with poor source-of-hire ROI[11]

evidence.gloss: Long time-to-fill inflates internal labor costs
evidence.verbatim: long time-to-fill that inflates internal labor costs[11]

evidence.gloss: No structured referral program means missing cheaper, higher-retention hires
evidence.verbatim: the absence of a structured referral program (referred hires reportedly cost 40–60% less than agency placements with higher retention)[11]

evidence.gloss: Unstructured multi-round interviews inflate hiring manager time costs
evidence.verbatim: unstructured, multi-round interview processes that inflate hiring manager time costs[11].

evidence.gloss: Offer decline: 100% of process cost with zero return
evidence.verbatim: Offer decline is flagged as a particularly costly and underappreciated failure mode: a declined offer represents 100% of process cost with zero return, and with 35% of candidates reported to have backed out even after accepting offers in Q1 2025, this waste is described as increasingly common[11].

evidence.gloss: Referred hires cost 40-60% less than agency placements and retain better
evidence.verbatim: referred hires cost 40-60% less than agency placements and retain better

h3.h3: Tools for calculating and comparing source-channel ROI

evidence.gloss: Gem's Source Channel ROI Calculator functionality
evidence.verbatim: Gem's Source Channel ROI Calculator lets teams add expense records (event, subscription, or per-hire fees) for each source and then sort sources by overall cost as well as cost per application and cost per hire, so recruiting teams can track spending trends and decide which sourcing methods to keep[16].

evidence.gloss: A third party builds a cost-per-hire formula around LinkedIn's list pricing
evidence.verbatim: Instead, a third-party source builds a cost-per-hire formula around LinkedIn's list pricing: (Annual seat cost + InMail overages + recruiter time cost) ÷ annual hires = cost per hire,

sections.h2: How should cost per hire be used in practice, not just calculated?

h3.h3: Why shouldn't cost per hire be read in isolation?

evidence.gloss: Checking correlation between spend and retention, quality, satisfaction
evidence.verbatim: Applying the metric further means checking correlation with other outcomes: whether higher per-hire spend for a given role or department corresponds to higher retention or quality ratings, and whether cutting per-application spend negatively affects candidate satisfaction or offer-acceptance rate[16].

evidence.gloss: Multiple sources caution against reading CPH in isolation
evidence.verbatim: Multiple sources caution against reading CPH in isolation.

evidence.gloss: CPH ignores quality of hire, time to fill, lost productivity
evidence.verbatim: It "ignores quality of hire, time to fill, and lost productivity, so do not read it alone"[3]

evidence.gloss: CPH needs complementary metrics since a rising figure could reflect quality investment not inefficiency
evidence.verbatim: and it "needs complementary metrics to be useful" since a rising CPH figure could just as easily reflect better recruiters, paid job boards, or ATS investment rather than inefficiency[15].

evidence.gloss: CPH framed as diagnostic tool, not a vanity metric
evidence.verbatim: One source frames the metric's proper use as diagnostic rather than evaluative: "cost per hire isn't a vanity metric. It's a diagnostic tool that reveals where your recruiting process leaks money,"

evidence.gloss: Recommended practice: track consistently, break down by channel, pair with quality metrics
evidence.verbatim: with the recommended practice being to track it consistently using the same methodology each period, break it down by channel to identify which sources convert to starts, and pair it with quality metrics so the organization isn't "optimising for cheap hires that don't stick"[16].

h3.h3: How often and how should cost per hire be reported?

evidence.gloss: review costs quarterly, not annually, since monthly data is noisy and annual data is too slow
evidence.verbatim: review costs quarterly rather than annually, since monthly data is noisy and annual data arrives too late to catch cost creep

evidence.gloss: comparing annual figures to a single quarter (or fractional FTEs) further distorts comparisons
evidence.verbatim: comparing an annual figure against a single quarter's hires (or counting fractional FTEs instead of whole hires) further distorts the comparison[6].

evidence.gloss: Quarterly reporting cadence recommended over monthly or annual
evidence.verbatim: Best-practice reporting applies a quarterly review cycle: monthly data is described as too noisy and annual data as arriving too late to correct course, while quarterly reporting surfaces cost creep before it compounds[6][8].

evidence.gloss: Recommended CPH reporting views
evidence.verbatim: Recommended reporting views include CPH trend over time (tracking cost changes across quarters and tying shifts to hiring volume or process changes), CPH by department and role level, CPH by sourcing channel, and CPH versus benchmarks and targets,

evidence.gloss: Outliers flagged for investigation rather than skewing averages
evidence.verbatim: with outliers (an unusually expensive executive search or an unusually cheap referral hire) flagged for investigation rather than left to skew averages[8].

evidence.gloss: CPH and CPA compared against industry standards
evidence.verbatim: Calculated CPH and CPA can be compared "to industry standards to see whether your company is hiring more or less efficiently than competitors"[16].

h3.h3: How is cost per hire used for budgeting and forecasting?

evidence.gloss: CPH's value lies in application, not as a static number
evidence.verbatim: Once a defensible cost-per-hire figure has been calculated, its value comes from how it is applied to budgeting, benchmarking, and process decisions rather than as a single static number.

evidence.gloss: CPH enables budgeting and forecasting future expenses
evidence.verbatim: A calculated CPH lets HR teams "budget for your recruitment process and even predict expenses for future talent needs"[14].

evidence.gloss: Separation rates plus CPH used to forecast replacement-hiring budget
evidence.verbatim: Applying these separation rates to headcount allows an organization to forecast the volume of replacement hires and, combined with a known CPH, project the associated budget need.

sections.h2: What Should a Cost-Per-Hire Framework and Checklist Include?

h3.h3: What the Framework Provides

evidence.gloss: Framework offers customizable templates per cost category
evidence.verbatim: One such framework offers "templates for each cost category with customizable line items"

evidence.gloss: Framework calculates CPH segmented by department, role, location, source channel
evidence.verbatim: states it "helps you calculate cost per hire segmented by department, role level, geographic location, and source channel,"

evidence.gloss: Framework includes benchmarking guidance using SHRM, Mercer, CUPA-HR data
evidence.verbatim: including "benchmarking guidance using SHRM, Mercer, and CUPA-HR data"

evidence.gloss: Framework offered as Detailed version (comprehensive, with benchmarking data and reduction strategies)
evidence.verbatim: a "Detailed version for a comprehensive hiring cost analysis and optimisation guide with granular category breakdowns, industry benchmarking data, and cost reduction strategies for each expense category"[8]

evidence.gloss: Framework's requested inputs list
evidence.verbatim: Inputs requested include "recruiting team size and compensation, technology platform costs, agency usage and fee structures, annual hiring volume by role level, and current sourcing channel mix,"

evidence.gloss: Framework frames CPH within a balanced TA scorecard (quality, speed, candidate experience, diversity)
evidence.verbatim: "framing cost-per-hire reporting within a balanced talent acquisition scorecard that also includes quality, speed, candidate experience, and diversity metrics"[8]

h3.h3: A Standardized Cost-Tracking Checklist

evidence.gloss: A 'Cost Per Hire Framework' checklist presents a standardised methodology based on ANSI/SHRM 06001-2012
evidence.verbatim: One source presents a full "Cost Per Hire Framework" as "a standardised methodology for capturing the true, fully-loaded expense of filling a single position," based explicitly on ANSI/SHRM 06001-2012[8].

evidence.gloss: Framework checklist item: cost-tracking system integrated with ATS/procurement/GL using standardized cost codes
evidence.verbatim: designing a cost-tracking system integrated with ATS/procurement/general-ledger systems using standardized cost codes;

evidence.gloss: Framework checklist item: requisition-level committed vs. actual cost capture
evidence.verbatim: requisition-level cost tracking with committed vs. actual cost capture (purchase order vs. invoice payment);

evidence.gloss: Framework checklist item: monthly data-collection cadence with named ownership and audits
evidence.verbatim: a monthly data-collection cadence with named ownership (talent acquisition ops for ATS data, finance for invoices, hiring managers for time estimates) plus automated reminders, escalation, and quarterly audits;

evidence.gloss: Framework checklist item: activity-based costing for shared costs like employer branding and overhead
evidence.verbatim: activity-based costing for allocating shared costs like employer branding campaigns and corporate overhead;

evidence.gloss: Framework checklist item: multi-year historical cost database for trend analysis and forecasting
evidence.verbatim: and a multi-year historical cost database for trend analysis and forecasting[8].

evidence.gloss: Framework instructs documenting methodology changes and restating prior periods for comparability
evidence.verbatim: It also instructs users to "document methodology changes and restate prior periods where material changes affect comparability," explicitly connecting the calculator's output back to auditable methodology rather than a one-off number[8].

evidence.gloss: Checklist: correlate CPH with quality-of-hire indicators to find diminishing returns point
evidence.verbatim: this framework's checklist includes correlating cost per hire with quality-of-hire indicators (performance ratings, 12-month retention, hiring-manager satisfaction) to find "the point of diminishing returns where additional spending does not significantly improve quality"[8]

evidence.gloss: Checklist: model CPH scenarios for budget planning
evidence.verbatim: modeling CPH scenarios for budget planning under different hiring-volume and agency-usage assumptions[8]

evidence.gloss: Checklist: build activity-based costing and allocation rules for shared costs
evidence.verbatim: building activity-based costing and allocation rules for shared costs (documented and applied consistently, with sensitivity analysis for judgment calls)[8]

evidence.gloss: Checklist: track costs at requisition level, committed vs actual
evidence.verbatim: tracking costs at the individual requisition level, capturing both committed costs (purchase order raised) and actual costs (invoice paid)[8]

h3.h3: Practical Recommendations for Tracking Cost Per Hire

evidence.gloss: Paychex 2026 survey: CPH is #1 tracked HR metric for small businesses
evidence.verbatim: On usage patterns, Paychex's 2026 Business Leaders Priorities survey found cost per hire is the #1 HR metric tracked by 47% of businesses with 5-19 employees and 54% of businesses with 20-49 employees[5].

evidence.verbatim: to track it on a quarterly cadence against trend, department/role level, sourcing channel, and benchmark/target views

evidence.verbatim: flagging outliers such as an unusually expensive executive search for separate investigation rather than folding them into an average[26].
